questions.q: At roughly 50 employees, what does this lesson say a typical identity architecture looks like?
options: Dozens of federated identity providers
No identity provider at all
A fully automated SCIM pipeline from day one
A single identity provider with a small number of apps connected via SAML or OIDC
questions.explain: At this scale, one IdP covers the whole company and SSO is a convenience rather than a necessity.

questions.q: What problem does SCIM-based provisioning solve as an organization grows?
options: It only works for a single application
It disables multi-factor authentication
It automates account creation, updates, and removal across connected apps, preventing accounts that should have been offboarded from being left active
It replaces the need for an identity provider entirely
questions.explain: SCIM provisioning pushes account lifecycle changes from the IdP to every connected app automatically, closing the manual-offboarding gap.

questions.q: What typically becomes the "source of truth" feeding identity data into the IdP as a company scales?
options: Each individual application's own user database
The company's firewall
A spreadsheet maintained by IT
The HR system
questions.explain: The HR system is the one that actually knows when someone joins, changes roles, or leaves, so it becomes the authoritative feed into the IdP.

questions.q: What real architecture decision does an acquisition typically force, according to this lesson?
options: Whether to consolidate the acquired company into a single IdP or federate the two identity providers
Whether to switch from SAML to OIDC with no other considerations
Whether to stop using SSO altogether
Whether to delete all user accounts immediately
questions.explain: An acquired company brings its own identity source, forcing a choice between consolidating into one IdP or federating the two with a trust relationship.

questions.q: What factors does this lesson say actually drive the single-IdP-vs-federation decision?
options: None — the decision is made randomly
Alphabetical order of company names
App count, compliance and data-residency requirements, and timeline pressure
Which identity provider has the nicest-looking login screen
questions.explain: The worked example weighs app count, compliance and data residency, and how much disruption a forced migration causes against timeline pressure.
